name: Fatima Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Northfield Packaging, we make cardboard boxes, the brown ones everything gets delivered in. I run the die-cutter, a big flatbed press that stamps the box shapes out of sheets of corrugated board. I set the cutting die, feed the stacks in, watch for crushed edges and jams, and clear the waste bits out from underneath. It's loud and dusty, and there's paper dust in everything, my hair, my lunchbox.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst part of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is when a run goes smoothly, twenty thousand boxes and not one reject, and Dariusz the supervisor gives you a nod. Worst part is the early starts in winter, and the pay, if I'm honest. Tomas, my boyfriend, drives a delivery van, so between us we cover the rent, but if one of us misses a week we're in trouble. I don't do the AI stuff, my phone's for messages and the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, fine, back to work. I'd probably say it to Dariusz on the break, something like 'see, all that fuss.' I'm not online much, maybe a thumbs up on someone's post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing changes, and that suits me. I like knowing what Monday looks like. The money's still tight, but that was true before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep doing my shifts and keep the overtime when it's offered. Maybe Tomas and I keep trying to put twenty a week aside, which never quite works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really, like a test got cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does putting twenty a week aside never quite work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something always comes up. Last month it was the van's insurance going up, before that my mum's washing machine. My mum's on her own with my two little brothers, so if she needs help I give it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work you'd want to change, if nothing else did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper heater near the press in winter. And maybe a bit more pay for the people who set the dies, because if you set it wrong you waste a whole stack. That's it. I'm not asking for much.

S0.say: She'd tell her supervisor 'see, all that fuss' and get back to work. She isn't online much, so maybe a thumbs up on someone's post.
S0.think: She thinks nothing changes, which suits her because she likes knowing what Monday looks like. Money stays tight, but that was true before AI.
S0.do: Keeps working her shifts and takes overtime when offered. Keeps trying, with Tomas, to put about twenty a week aside.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a cancelled test.
S0.quote: I like knowing what Monday looks like.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima values routine above almost anything and was openly relieved. She supports her mother and two younger brothers, which explains why savings never build. Her wishes for work were small and practical: a heater and fair pay for die-setters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen whether we like it or not, so the company had better be fair about it. I wouldn't go on about it, I'd just ask Dariusz what's coming. That's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is one they'd go for. There are already machines that feed and strip the die-cutter automatically, I've seen them at the bigger plant. If Northfield buys one, they need one person for two presses, and I'm not the one who's good with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well, so they want to keep me. Tomas and I would stop eating out at all and cancel the gym I never go to. I wouldn't sign up for courses, I'd just hope I'm one of the people they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knotted up. It sits in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hope they keep you. What if they offered training on the new machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it if they said I had to. I wouldn't put my hand up. I'm slow with new things, and I hate looking stupid in front of the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did lose the job, where would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's the frozen food place on the industrial estate and the supermarket. That's about it around here. The frozen food place has its own robots coming, Tomas delivers there, he says they're half automatic already.

S1.say: She'd say the change will happen anyway, so the company must be fair about it. She wouldn't make a fuss, she'd just ask her supervisor what's coming.
S1.think: She thinks her job is a likely target because auto-feeding die-cutters already exist at a bigger plant. If one person ends up running two presses, she fears it won't be her, since she isn't good with screens.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and works hard so the company wants to keep her. Cuts eating out and cancels her unused gym membership, and avoids signing up for courses unless required.
S1.feel: Knotted up, sitting in her stomach.
S1.quote: I wouldn't put my hand up. I'm slow with new things, and I hate looking stupid in front of the younger ones.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima's resistance to training comes from fear of embarrassment more than dislike of change. She thinks in terms of being chosen to stay rather than choosing a path. Local alternatives are few and also automating, according to her boyfriend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what anyone's supposed to do with two years. I'd ask at work what the plan is, and I'd expect nobody to know. I'd stay quiet online, I wouldn't know what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd both be out of work, me and Tomas. If robots can do hands-on work, they can stamp boxes and drive vans. We have maybe two weeks' money, and my mum leans on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably freeze for a bit, if I'm honest. Then I'd look for anything at all, cleaning, shop work, whatever's still human. We'd give up the flat and move in with my mum, which means three adults and two boys in a three-bedroom place, and I'd sign up for any help going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. Like being in a crowd and not finding the exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, is there anything that would help you move faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone telling me exactly what to do. A person, not a website. I'm good when I know the steps. I'm useless when it's 'figure it out yourself'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brothers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're twelve and fifteen. I'd tell them to stay in school and not to worry, and then I'd go in the bathroom and worry. The fifteen-year-old wants to be a mechanic, and I wouldn't know what to say to that.

S2.say: She'd say she has no idea what anyone could do with two years and would ask at work, expecting nobody to have a plan. She'd stay quiet online.
S2.think: She believes both she and Tomas would lose their jobs, since robots could stamp boxes and drive vans. With two weeks of money and her mother relying on her, she sees no buffer.
S2.do: Freezes at first, then looks for any work that still needs people, such as cleaning or shop work. Gives up the flat to move in with her mother and signs up for any help available.
S2.feel: Panicky, like being stuck in a crowd with no exit.
S2.quote: I'd tell them to stay in school and not to worry, and then I'd go in the bathroom and worry.
S2.fieldNote: Fatima admitted she would freeze, which fits her resistance to change. She said she does well with clear steps from a person, not online self-help. The worry about her younger brothers, especially the one who wants to be a mechanic, felt deeply personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. Companies and the government should use it to tell people like me where the jobs will be. I'd say that to Dariusz, and maybe at the job centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know myself. I'd spend the first two years hoping it isn't true. Then I'd be panicking in year four, which is basically the two-year version, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to make myself start something small in the first year, like the forklift licence, because Dariusz has said they need more drivers. Tomas and I would save hard, no holidays, no new phone. And I'd want my mum to have a plan too, maybe she could get some work while she still can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in a slow way. Less like a crowd, more like a dripping tap you can't turn off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend two years hoping it isn't true. What would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it at Northfield. If they wheeled in a robot feeder, that would make it real. Things on the news don't feel real to me until they're in the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change anything about you and Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about getting engaged. I'd still do it, it doesn't cost much if you don't make it fancy. But a house, kids, all that, I'd put on hold until I know what we're both doing.

S3.say: She'd say five years at least gives companies and government time to tell workers where jobs will be. She'd raise it with her supervisor and at the job centre.
S3.think: She knows she'd likely spend two years hoping it isn't true, then panic in year four. She sees that as the fast version, only delayed.
S3.do: Pushes herself to get a forklift licence in the first year, since her supervisor says drivers are needed. Saves hard with Tomas by skipping holidays and a new phone, and encourages her mother to find work while she can.
S3.feel: A slow worry, like a dripping tap she can't turn off.
S3.quote: Things on the news don't feel real to me until they're in the building.
S3.fieldNote: Fatima was strikingly self-aware: she predicted her own denial and late panic. Change becomes real for her only when it physically arrives at Northfield. She'd still get engaged but would put a house and children on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it properly, so there's no excuse for anyone. I'd say people should be told early and given help to move. Not much online, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years is the only one where someone like me actually changes. Even I can't pretend for ten years. By the middle of it, the robots would be in the building, and that would push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the five-year one, the forklift licence first. Then maybe I'd go for something with people, my aunt does home care and says they're always short. I'd want Tomas and me to have three months saved by the time it lands, and I'd try to stop lending mum money for anything except emergencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still, but it's a worry I can live with. It's not the bathroom-door kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say even you can't pretend for ten years. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. But I'd have Tomas nagging me and my aunt nagging me, and eventually I do what I'm nagged into. That's how I learned to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after it arrives, in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven. I don't know what work there'd be. I can only see the ten years before it. After that I just hope somebody has worked it out, because I won't have.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuse, and people should be warned early and helped to move. She'd post little online, as usual.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is the only version where someone like her would really change, because she can't stay in denial that long. Robots in the building by mid-decade would push her.
S4.do: Gets a forklift licence first, then considers home care, where her aunt says staff are short. Aims for three months of savings with Tomas and limits lending money to her mother to emergencies.
S4.feel: Worried, but a worry she can live with.
S4.quote: Eventually I do what I'm nagged into. That's how I learned to drive.
S4.fieldNote: Fatima sees long warning as the only way she would really change, mostly through pressure from her partner and aunt. Her honesty about not seeing past 2036 felt genuine. She plans to set a limit on helping her mother, which seemed hard for her to say.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time for me to stop hoping and start doing. What would help is a real person who tells me the steps, here's the course, here's the job at the end, here's the money to live on while you do it. Not an app.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about families like mine, where one person's wage holds up a few people. If I go down, my mum and my brothers feel it too. It's never just one job.

headlineQuote: If I go down, my mum and my brothers feel it too. It's never just one job.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old die-cutter operator at a cardboard box factory, living with her boyfriend Tomas, a delivery driver, and helping support her mother and two younger brothers on very little savings. She loves routine, avoids technology and fears looking slow in front of younger workers. She doesn't blame anyone in particular and mostly hopes to be one of the people the company keeps. She is open about her own pattern of denial followed by late panic, so the fast AGI scenario overwhelms her, while ten years is the only version where she thinks she would really change.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time for her to stop hoping and start acting.
whatWouldHelp: A real person who lays out the steps: the course, the job at the end of it, and money to live on while she trains, not an app.
